newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy reform body rejects centre-left amendment.
newsitem.headline: Italy reform body rejects centre-left amendment.

text.p: Italy's cross-party constitutional reform commission on Tuesday approved proposals for parliamentary changes and rejected an amendment put forward by the centre-left on a two-round electoral system.

The rejection was a setback for the centre-left, already outvoted in the commission by centre-right parties who have succeeded in getting backing for a directly-elected president to govern alongside a parliamentary premier.
The commission, headed by the leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) Massimo D'Alema, must vote on a package of proposals covering five main areas by June 30.
The agreed basic texts then go before both houses of parliament for further debate and modification.
The centre-left had wanted a two-round system at constituency level between parties in general elections.
They wanted a candidate to be elected in the first round if he or she won more than 50 percent of the vote.
Failing that, a second round would be held between leading candidates with the winner to be elected.
The centre-right had instead wanted a second round between the two leading coalitions for a given number of seats.
The centre-left proposal was rejected, prompting delight among the centre-right opposition.
"There is truly a constituent climate," said opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi. "The vote is not expressed according to starting positions but according to one's own convictions.
"This second round between coalitions will push parties with the same values, the same programmes, to stay together over and above individual candidates."

Pierferdinando Casini, leader of the small CCD party in Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance coalition, said that the decision on the second round meant a positive outcome to the commission stage was now far more likely.
"This is a positive fact without any doubt," he said.
D'Alema had said earlier that the centre-left's amendment offered the chance to "send a very strong signal, a clear signal of change to the country."

The commission was set up earlier this year to map out constitutional reform that would introduce more lasting administrations and end the revolving-door governments that have plagued Italy since World War Two.
Regarding the structure of parliament, the commission agreed on the need for smaller upper and lower houses with younger members than allowed at present.
The proposal was for the Chamber of deputies (lower house) to be reduced to 400 deputies from 630 with admission from the age of 21 instead of 25 at present.
The upper house would be trimmed to 200 from 315 senators aged 35 and upwards, a five year drop in ages.
A special commission for autonomous regions would also be set up, made up of senators, regional presidents and representatives of local government.
The commission also proposed measures to make referendums harder, suggesting raising the number of signatures required.
